title: safehaven: Hedge and Safe Haven Testing in R
text: The safehaven package tests the hedge and safe haven hypotheses (Baur, D. G., T. K. McDermott, 2010), estimates hedge ratios, hedging effectiveness and optimal portfolio weights (Basher, S. A., P. Sadorsky, 2016), and computes the conditional diversification benefit (Christoffersen, P., V. Errunza, K. Jacobs, H. Langlois, 2012; Christoffersen, P., K. Jacobs, X. Jin, H. Langlois, 2018). This guide also shows how to complement these with cross-quantilogram-based predictability (Han, H., O. Linton, T. Oka, Y.-J. Whang, 2016).

title: safehaven: Hedge and Safe Haven Testing in R
text:
Background
The role of assets such as gold and bitcoin as potential hedges or safe havens for equity markets has attracted increasing scholarly attention (e.g., Ali, S., E. Bouri, R. L. Czudaj, S. J. H. Shahzad (2020); Shahzad, S. J. H., E. Bouri, D. Roubaud, L. Kristoufek, B. Lucey (2019); Shahzad, S. J. H., E. Bouri, D. Roubaud, L. Kristoufek (2020); Mujtaba, G., A. Siddique, N. Naifar, S. J. H. Shahzad (2024)), particularly in periods of heightened economic uncertainty, persistent inflation and shifting monetary policy.
Following Baur, D. G., T. K. McDermott (2010), an asset is a

hedge if it is uncorrelated (weak) or negatively correlated (strong) with the market on average;
safe haven if it is uncorrelated (weak) or negatively correlated (strong) with the market during extreme market declines.

title: safehaven: Hedge and Safe Haven Testing in R
text:
Example workflow: gold and bitcoin
We assess gold (GLD) and bitcoin (BTC) as potential hedges or safe havens for the U.S. stock market (S&P 500) using the bundled hedgedata dataset.

1. Hedge / safe-haven regression and classification

library(safehaven)
data("hedgedata")

# S&P 500 and gold
res_gld <- safe_haven_test(hedgedata$SP, hedgedata$GLD)
res_gld

  Hedge Coefficient     p_value
1    c0  0.02854200 0.243328427
2  0.10 -0.09181858 0.110421436
3  0.05 -0.12474223 0.001372538
4  0.01  0.05556154 0.238446604

# S&P 500 and bitcoin
res_btc <- safe_haven_test(hedgedata$SP, hedgedata$BTC)
res_btc

  Hedge Coefficient      p_value
1    c0   0.7363518 2.508433e-15
2  0.10   0.7685085 5.144017e-04
3  0.05   0.9992671 1.846179e-10
4  0.01   1.7624203 2.752659e-32

# Classification
classify_safe_haven(res_gld)

Weak hedge; weak safe haven at 10% and 1%; strong safe haven at 5%. 

classify_safe_haven(res_btc)

Not a hedge; not a safe haven at 10%, 5% and 1%. 


c0 is the average-market coefficient; the rows 0.10, 0.05 and 0.01 are the cumulative coefficients when S&P 500 returns fall in their lower 10%, 5% and 1% quantiles.


2. Hedge ratio and hedging effectiveness via DCC

# Hedging asset: gold
dcc_hedge(hedgedata$SP, hedgedata$GLD)

     beta_mean   beta_min beta_max         HE       OPW
1 -0.004473511 -0.9198528 1.115682 0.02663489 0.4728486

# Hedging asset: bitcoin
dcc_hedge(hedgedata$SP, hedgedata$BTC)

   beta_mean    beta_min  beta_max         HE       OPW
1 0.05505125 -0.07302479 0.3868332 0.09587392 0.0277494


The output summarises the time-varying hedge ratio, the hedging effectiveness (HE) and the average optimal portfolio weight (OPW) of the hedging asset, as in Basher, S. A., P. Sadorsky (2016).


3. Cross-quantile dependence heatmaps
This step uses the quantilogram package (install.packages("quantilogram")).

library(quantilogram)
set.seed(123)

k      <- 1                    # lag order
vec.q  <- seq(0.1, 0.9, 0.1)   # quantiles
B.size <- 100                  # bootstrap repetitions

# Shared styling: the cross-quantilogram values are small, so the colour
# scale saturates at +/-0.05; bold values are significant at 5%.
heatmap <- function(df, var1, var2) {
  res <- crossq.heatmap(
    df, k, vec.q, B.size,
    var1_name = var1, var2_name = var2,
    title = paste("Cross-quantilogram:", var1, "vs", var2),
    subtitle = "Lag 1; bold = significant at 5%",
    colors = c("#2166AC", "#67A9CF", "white", "#EF8A62", "#B2182B"),
    color_values = c(-1, -0.05, 0, 0.05, 1),
    tile_border_color = "white", tile_border_width = 0.3, x_angle = 0
  )
  res$plot
}


# Gold (GLD) as predicted variable, S&P 500 (SP) as predicting variable
heatmap(hedgedata[, c("GLD", "SP")], "Gold", "S&P 500")









# Bitcoin (BTC) as predicted variable, S&P 500 (SP) as predicting variable
heatmap(hedgedata[, c("BTC", "SP")], "Bitcoin", "S&P 500")








The heatmaps show how dependence between the S&P 500 and gold or bitcoin varies across quantiles, indicating whether the hedging asset remains uncorrelated or negatively correlated during market stress.


4. Diversification benefit

# S&P 500 / gold portfolio, 90% in the S&P 500, 5% tail
diversification_benefit(hedgedata$SP, hedgedata$GLD, p = 0.05, w = 0.90)

[1] 0.3011936

# S&P 500 / bitcoin portfolio, 90% in the S&P 500, 5% tail
diversification_benefit(hedgedata$SP, hedgedata$BTC, p = 0.05, w = 0.90)

[1] 0.5089053


w is the weight on the first asset (here the S&P 500). The measure lies between 0 (no diversification benefit, as with perfectly correlated assets) and 1; higher values imply stronger diversification benefits.

I am a Professor of Finance and Technology at the University of Waikato and Convenor of the Bachelor of Banking and Technology programme. Previously, I served as Associate Professor of Finance and Head of the Master of Science in Finance and Technology programmes at MBS School of Business, France.
My research focuses on asset pricing, climate finance, digital finance, sustainable investing, financial connectedness, and quantitative methods. title: Connectedness Approach in Financial Systems
text:
The connectedness approach (Diebold, F. X., K. Yilmaz, 2012; Diebold, F. X., K. Yilmaz, 2014) is a popular framework for understanding the transmission of shocks across assets or economic variables. It is based on the generalized forecast error variance decomposition (Pesaran, H. H., Y. Shin, 1998) of a vector autoregressive (VAR) model, which measures how much of the forecast error variance of one variable is explained by shocks to others.
While widely used, interpretation of connectedness measures requires care—especially in financial contexts where correlations (signed relationships) often guide investment and risk management decisions.

The connectedness approach is a popular framework for understanding the transmission of shocks across assets or economic variables. It is typically based on the variance decomposition of a vector autoregressive (VAR) model, which measures how much of the forecast error variance of one variable is explained by shocks to others.
While widely used, interpretation of connectedness measures requires care—especially in financial contexts where correlations (signed relationships) often guide investment and risk management decisions.

title: Connectedness Approach in Financial Systems
section: Variance vs. correlation: why the sign matters
text:
Variance vs. correlation: why the sign matters
Variance and covariance are inherently unsigned measures of association. They capture the magnitude of dependence, but not its direction. In contrast, correlation provides a signed indicator of whether assets tend to move together (positive correlation) or in opposite directions (negative correlation).
As a result, connectedness metrics—being variance-based—do not distinguish between risk comovement and hedging (safe-haven) behavior. For example:

A strong stock–gold connectedness does not necessarily imply risk transmission. Gold may act as a safe haven, moving inversely with stocks during crises.
Similarly, stock–bond or stock–uncertainty pairs often exhibit negative correlations. Without considering the expected sign, high connectedness could be misinterpreted as contagion, when it may actually reflect diversification.

title: Connectedness Approach in Financial Systems
Connectedness Approach in Financial Systems
text:
Recommendations

Use the connectedness approach only when the system variables have theoretically consistent relationships.
Avoid mixing assets with fundamentally opposite expected signs (e.g., stock–gold) unless you explicitly address sign effects.
Consider supplementing variance-based connectedness with correlation or coherence analysis to capture directionality.
Always interpret connectedness in the context of economic theory and empirical sign expectations.

This limitation applies to all variants of the approach, including asymmetric, quantile, time-varying parameter (TVP), R² and R² quantile connectedness measures.

title: Connectedness Approach in Financial Systems
text:
Minimal Demo of Note

set.seed(123)

library(zoo)
library(ConnectednessApproach)

# -------------------------------
# Positive correlation case
# -------------------------------
n   <- 1000
idx <- seq(as.Date("2010-01-01"), by = "day", length.out = n)

x <- rnorm(n)
y <- 0.5 * x + rnorm(n, 0, 0.2)

df_p <- zoo(cbind(x, y), order.by = idx)

fit_p <- VAR(df_p, configuration = list(nlag = 4, method = "pearson"))
dca_p <- TimeConnectedness(
  Phi         = fit_p$B,
  Sigma       = fit_p$Q,
  nfore       = 10,
  generalized = TRUE
)

# Correlation
